title: actionkv: a log-structured key-value store
summary: Rust in Action's actionkv: the key-value model, the Bitcask record format, an append-only log with an in-memory index, loading by scanning, insert, get with seek, update and delete with tombstones, why append-only survives crashes, compaction, and choosing between HashMap and BTreeMap for the index.

blocks.title: Why append-only?
blocks.md: Old data is never overwritten, so a crash in the middle of a write can only damage the **last** record, and its checksum reveals that. Appending is also the fastest way to write to a disk. The costs: the file grows with every update, and the index must be rebuilt by scanning the log on startup (or saved separately, which is what *Rust in Action*'s `akv_disk` does).

blocks.title: The record format
blocks.md: Each record is the format from the previous lesson: a 12-byte header of little-endian `u32`s (CRC32 checksum, key length, value length), then the key and the value. *Rust in Action* reads it with the `byteorder` and `crc` crates; below, the same logic uses only the standard library. `process_record` accepts any `Read`, so it works on files and on byte slices.

blocks.output:
Fiji -> Suva
Kiribati -> Tarawa
Cook Islands not found
5 records on disk, 132 bytes
blocks.explain: After reopening, `load` replays the whole log: later records for the same key overwrite earlier positions in the index, so the update and the tombstone win. Five records are on disk even though only two keys are alive; that waste is what compaction removes.

steps.title: open + load: O(size of the log)
steps.md: Read every record once and remember the newest position per key. This is the price of not saving the index.

steps.title: insert / update / delete: one append
steps.md: Seek to the end, write header and body, flush. No existing byte is touched.

steps.title: get: one hash lookup and one seek
steps.md: The index gives the position; `seek` jumps there and `process_record` reads one record, checking its checksum.

steps.title: compaction: rewrite live records
steps.md: Copy only the records the index points to (and skip tombstones) into a new file, then rename it over the old one. Real systems do this in the background.

blocks.title: HashMap or BTreeMap for the index?
blocks.md: Both store key-value pairs. A **`HashMap`** hashes the key to find a bucket: lookups are O(1) on average, but iteration order is arbitrary. A **`BTreeMap`** keeps keys **sorted** in a B-tree: lookups are O(log n), iteration is in order, and **range queries** are possible. *Rust in Action*'s rule: use `HashMap` unless you need ordering or ranges.

blocks.title: A tiny in-memory log
blocks.md: Without files: keep the log as a `Vec<(String, Option<String>)>` (None is a tombstone) and an index `HashMap<String, usize>` of positions. Implement `set`, `del` and `get`, then `compact`, which builds a new log with only live entries and a fresh index.

blocks.title: actionkv over any storage
blocks.goal: Implement the log-structured store generically over Read + Write + Seek so it runs on files and in memory, with crash safety and compaction.
blocks.behavior:
`pub struct ActionKV<F: Read + Write + Seek> { f: F, pub index: HashMap<Vec<u8>, u64> }`. Records use the Bitcask layout: `[crc32 u32 LE][key_len u32 LE][val_len u32 LE][key][value]`, the checksum covering key + value.
- `pub fn open(f: F) -> io::Result<Self>`: scan the whole log from the start, building the index. A clean end (no bytes left) stops the scan. A **truncated last record** (a crash during a write) also stops it: ignore that partial record. A record whose checksum is wrong is an error of kind `InvalidData`.
- The index holds **live keys only**: a tombstone (a record with an empty value) removes its key from the index, both in `delete` and while scanning in `open` (as in *Rust in Action*, storing an empty value therefore means deleting).
- `pub fn get(&mut self, key: &[u8]) -> io::Result<Option<Vec<u8>>>`: seek to the indexed position and read that record.
- `pub fn insert`, `update` (same as insert) and `delete` (appends a tombstone; deleting a missing key does nothing and writes nothing).
- `pub fn len(&self) -> usize`: the number of live keys.
- `pub fn compact<G: Read + Write + Seek>(&mut self, into: G) -> io::Result<ActionKV<G>>`: write only the live records, in sorted key order, to `into` and return a store over it.
- `pub fn into_inner(self) -> F`.

examples.input: insert a=1, insert b=2, update a=3, delete b; reopen; get a

hints: Write with `self.f.seek(SeekFrom::End(0))?` and remember that position: it is where the record starts.
In `open`, read the 12-byte header with `read_exact`. `UnexpectedEof` on the header or the body means a clean end or a torn write: stop.
While scanning: `if value.is_empty() { index.remove(&key); } else { index.insert(key, pos); }`.
Compaction: collect the index keys into a `Vec`, sort it, `get` each one and insert the live ones into `ActionKV::open(into)?`.
blocks.solution_explain: The store never assumes a file: `Cursor<Vec<u8>>` in the tests, `File` in a real program. Treating `UnexpectedEof` while reading as the end of the log is what makes a torn last write harmless; a checksum mismatch in a complete record is real corruption and is reported.

questions.q: How does actionkv update a value?
options: Overwrites the old record in place
Appends a new record and points the index at it
Deletes the file and rewrites it
The record is removed from the file
A tombstone: a record with an empty value
questions.explanation: So a reload knows the key is gone.

questions.q: Why does an append-only log survive crashes well?
options: Existing data is never overwritten, so only the last record can be damaged, and its checksum shows it
questions.explanation: Torn writes affect only the tail.

questions.q: What does the in-memory index store?
options: For each key, the byte position of its latest record

questions.q: When should the index be a BTreeMap rather than a HashMap?
options: When you need keys in order or range queries

points: A key-value store maps byte keys to byte values with get, insert, update and delete.
actionkv appends Bitcask records (checksum, lengths, key, value) and keeps an index of positions in memory.
Updates append; deletes append tombstones; loading replays the log so the latest record wins.
Append-only logs are crash-friendly and fast to write but grow until compacted.
Writing against Read + Write + Seek lets the same store run on files and in memory.
